summary: Expanded Related Work to cover evidence reranking, compact graph retrieval, and complementary drug-repositioning approaches, and clarified the contribution (manuscript pp. 3–4).
Added learned and automatically selected coefficients, equal-weight controls, and cross-dataset transfer (manuscript Section 4.5, p. 14; Supplementary Section S12, pp. 18–23).
Added matched-budget subgraph comparisons and quantitative retention analyses (manuscript Section 4.6, p. 15; Supplementary Section S13, pp. 23–28).
Clarified the fixed-candidate evaluation scope and updated numerical reporting (manuscript Section 4.2, pp. 11–12; manuscript Table 3, p. 13).
Documented repoDB preprocessing, entity alignment, and leakage control (manuscript Section 4.1, pp. 10–11; Supplementary Section S11.1, pp. 17–18).
Refined the discussion of multi-source fusion, the limitations, and the conclusions (manuscript Section 5, pp. 17–18; Section 6, pp. 18–19).

1: We thank the reviewer for highlighting the need for clearer positioning. Related Work now discusses RankRAG, G-Retriever, GRAG, and SubgraphRAG, explaining their approaches to context ranking, compact graph retrieval, and learned triple selection (manuscript pp. 3–4, particularly Section 2.3, p. 4).

We have revised the novelty claims to emphasize the integration of biomedical evidence cues for candidate reranking and graph selection. The contribution centers on graded support, shortcut and contradiction penalties, and rank-preserving evidence selection, building on established reranking and retrieval principles. This scope is stated in the manuscript Abstract (p. 1), Introduction contributions (p. 3), Discussion (pp. 17–18), and Conclusion (pp. 18–19).
2: We thank the reviewer for this concern. We added validation-based coefficient search, a learned scorer using five shared features, and leave-one-dataset-out (LODO) transfer that excludes target calibration labels. Learning uses a regularized pairwise objective with query-group cross-validation; equal-weight controls isolate the effect of learning. For fuzzy retrieval, automatic selection compares 12 coefficient vectors at fixed candidate order and graph budget. All coefficient selection precedes test evaluation.

Learned weights improve candidate MRR over the original formula on four datasets and match it on PrimeKG; LODO gives higher point estimates on all five. Against equal weights, the learned gain on repoDB is 0.00754, with an exploratory 95% interval of [0.00040, 0.01518]; the other four intervals include zero. These findings support coefficient reuse within the evaluated benchmarks, with dataset-dependent benefits.

The main findings appear in manuscript Section 4.5 (p. 14) and manuscript Table 4 (p. 15). Supplementary Section S12 (pp. 18–23) and Supplementary Tables S16–S24 (pp. 19–23) provide the fitting, transfer, ablation, and sensitivity analyses.
3: We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. Across all five datasets, we compared fuzzy retrieval with random sampling, coverage-based, score-based, breadth-first, PageRank, shortest-path, and relation-stratified selectors, fixing candidate order and the unique-edge budget. The analyses measure candidate coverage, reachability, labeled paths, and encoder representations across multiple budgets. Matched-budget random controls use five seeds, with query-cluster bootstrap intervals for uncertainty.

Fuzzy retrieval preserves incident evidence for all source-covered candidates, while three-hop reachability retention ranges from 0.4835 on Hetionet to 0.9546 on repoDB. It exceeds random selection on PharmKG, DRKG, and repoDB. Shortest-path selection retains more connectivity but covers fewer candidates on some datasets. The path-level analysis also finds no retained length-three paths on eligible PharmKG and Hetionet rows, although shorter paths can remain. These results distinguish candidate coverage from preservation of connected evidence.

Manuscript Section 4.6 and manuscript Table 5 (both p. 15) summarize these findings. Supplementary Section S13 (pp. 23–28), Supplementary Tables S25–S29 (pp. 25–26), and Supplementary Figs. S4–S6 (pp. 27–28) provide the detailed comparisons.
4: We thank the reviewer for drawing attention to the evaluation scope. Soft support reorders the backbone’s fixed top-20 candidates, while fuzzy retrieval selects evidence without changing their membership or selected order. A gold drug outside that set remains unrecoverable. On PrimeKG, candidate MRR@20 increases from 0.0646 to 0.1253 at unchanged Gold@20 of 0.240, while fuzzy retrieval reduces the graph from 59.93 to 32.34 triples. These results support ranking and evidence-efficiency gains at fixed candidate coverage. We clarify this scope in manuscript Section 4.2 (pp. 11–12), with results in manuscript Table 3 (p. 13).

During revision, we corrected FP16 overflow affecting 9/500 PrimeKG full-graph test cases and standardized E2E scoring. Re-evaluation used FP32 graph encoding and BF16 inference with unchanged checkpoints and splits and no excluded cases; for example, the source E2E MRR changed from 0.0476 to 0.0477 (manuscript Table 3, p. 13).

We also recalculated validation candidate MRR from candidate identifiers, assigning zero reciprocal rank to absent gold entities. The corrected values appear in manuscript Fig. 2 (p. 8), Supplementary Section S1.1 (pp. 3–4), Supplementary Table S6 (p. 11), and Supplementary Table S13 (p. 15).
5: We thank the reviewer for identifying this missing detail. We retain repoDB diseases as local UMLS nodes and join DRKG molecular evidence through exact DrugBank compound identifiers, preserving gene identifiers and relations. No disease crosswalk or disease-to-gene conversion is applied. In the prepared DRKG map, 1,130 of 1,571 compounds match; unmatched compounds remain in the task. None of the 2,051 disease CUIs has an exact identifier match, so disease-side alignment remains limited.

The evidence graph combines approved training pairs, conflict-cleaned diagnostic pairs, and compound–gene and gene–gene edges. Holdout requires both entities to remain represented in training, and held-out target triples are excluded from the evidence graph.

Manuscript Section 4.1 (pp. 10–11, repoDB paragraph on p. 11) describes the alignment. Supplementary Section S11.1 (pp. 17–18) details normalization, deduplication, label conflicts, graph construction, and splitting. Supplementary Table S15 (p. 17) distinguishes local graph-ID coverage from cross-resource alignment.
6: We thank the reviewer for highlighting these relevant studies. Related Work discusses spatial–spectral fusion and FD-MSGL in manuscript Section 2.1 (pp. 3–4); both are included as manuscript References 45–46 (p. 23). Their use of complementary biological networks provides context for representing associations that may be missed by a single evidence source.

The final paragraph of the manuscript Discussion (Section 5, p. 18) explains how jointly learning molecular, interaction, and pathway representations with fusion weights could enrich candidate scoring and guide graph selection under edge-budget and path-retention objectives. This direction would require consistent entity alignment and held-out evaluation to assess its benefits.
